orig_9709_p3_trig_reciprocal_functions.description: Read secant, cosecant and cotangent graphs, recognise their restrictions and use reciprocal identities.

sections.title: What am I taking the reciprocal of?
sections.label: Work with reciprocals
sections.intro: For an angle \(x\), take the reciprocal of cosine for secant and of sine for cosecant. For cotangent, use cosine divided by sine. Write the original denominator before substituting a value.

blocks.html: \(\sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x}\), \(\cosec x=\frac{1}{\sin x}\), \(\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\). These are reciprocal ratios. They do not return angles.
\(\cot x=\frac1{\tan x}\) where both expressions exist. At \(x=\frac\pi2\), tangent is undefined but \(\cot x=0\) from \(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\).

blocks.title: Read the signs before inverting
blocks.prompt: Find \(\cosec\frac{11\pi}{6}\) and \(\sec\frac{2\pi}{3}\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Both original ratios are negative. Find each one before taking its reciprocal.
blocks.solution: \(\sin\frac{11\pi}{6}=-\frac12\) and \(\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac12\), so both reciprocals are \(-2\).

retry.feedback: Sine is negative in quadrant IV.
This is the sine. Take its reciprocal.
Cosine is negative in quadrant II.

sections.title: Where do the reciprocal graphs break or cross?
sections.label: Read the graphs
sections.intro: Mark every zero of the denominator before drawing a curve. Each of these inputs gives a vertical asymptote. Where sine or cosine is \(1\) or \(-1\), its reciprocal has the same value.

blocks.html: Secant and cosecant have period \(2\pi\) and range \(y\le-1\) or \(y\ge1\). Cotangent has period \(\pi\) and takes every real value on each branch.

figure.alt: Three graphs on the same angular scale. Secant has asymptotes at pi over two and three pi over two. Cosecant and cotangent have asymptotes at zero, pi and two pi. Secant and cosecant have gaps between heights minus one and one. Cotangent crosses zero at pi over two and three pi over two.
figure.caption: Dashed vertical lines mark excluded inputs. The dashed horizontal guides are \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\). The plots use radians.

blocks.html: For integer \(k\), the secant poles are \(x=\frac\pi2+k\pi\). Both cosecant and cotangent have poles at \(x=k\pi\). Cotangent vanishes at \(x=\frac\pi2+k\pi\).

blocks.title: Locate the secant asymptotes
blocks.prompt: Give all values of \(x\) in \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\) where \(y=\sec x\) has a vertical asymptote.
blocks.hint: Start with the zeros of \(\cos x\).
blocks.solution: The asymptotes occur at \(x=-\frac\pi2\) and \(x=\frac\pi2\).

retry.feedback: The cosine at zero is one, so secant is defined there.
Cosine is even. Check both sides of zero.

sections.title: How can I connect squares of the ratios?
sections.label: Use the reciprocal identities
sections.intro: Start with \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\). Dividing every term by \(\cos^2x\) gives the secant identity. Dividing every term by \(\sin^2x\) gives the cosecant identity.

blocks.html: \(1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x\) where \(\cos x\ne0\). Also \(1+\cot^2 x=\cosec^2 x\) where \(\sin x\ne0\).
A squared identity gives a magnitude. Use the quadrant or the signs of the original ratios to decide the sign.

blocks.title: Use the quadrant to choose the sign
blocks.prompt: Angle \(x\) is in quadrant II and \(\cosec x=\frac{13}{5}\). Find \(\cot x\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use \(\cot^2 x=\cosec^2 x-1\). In quadrant II, cosine is negative and sine is positive.

retry.feedback: The identity gives the square. The signs of sine and cosine make cotangent negative here.

sections.title: How do I turn a reciprocal equation into a familiar one?
sections.label: Solve a reciprocal equation
sections.intro: For \(\sec x=k\) or \(\cosec x=k\), check \(|k|\ge1\) before taking reciprocals. For non-zero \(k\), \(\cot x=k\) gives \(\tan x=\frac1k\). If \(k=0\), use \(\cos x=0\) with \(\sin x\ne0\).

blocks.html: Work in the units of the interval. Using \(\pi\) for a period signals radians.

blocks.title: Use a negative tangent and repeat its period
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cot x=-\sqrt3\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\). Give all answers exactly.
blocks.hint: Use \(\tan x=-\frac1{\sqrt3}\), then move by \(\pi\) from the negative reference solution.
blocks.solution: One solution is \(-\frac\pi6\). Adding \(\pi\) gives \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\). Both have non-zero sine and lie in the given interval.

retry.feedback: Cotangent repeats every pi radians. Find the second angle in the interval.

sections.title: How does a horizontal shift move the exclusions?
sections.label: Shift the poles
sections.intro: Solve for the zeros of the denominator using the full shifted argument.

blocks.html: Use the original angle interval before mapping solutions back. The shift can bring a pole across an endpoint.
The numerator of a reciprocal is constant, so numerator zeros do not produce poles.

blocks.title: Find both exclusions for a shifted reciprocal
blocks.prompt: For \(0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\), find all inputs where \(\cot\left((x - 30)^\circ\right)\) is undefined. Enter angles in degrees.
blocks.hint: Only zeros of the denominator cause exclusions.
blocks.solution:
The denominator is \(\sin\left((x - 30)^\circ\right)\). List its zeros in the shifted interval.

Adding back the shift gives \(30^\circ\), \(210^\circ\).

glossary.definition: A line the graph approaches. At a vertical asymptote the function grows without bound on at least one side.
The smallest positive angle increment that repeats the graph.

examples.title: Evaluate reciprocal ratios in different quadrants
examples.question: Find \(\sec\frac{5\pi}{3}\), \(\cosec\frac{7\pi}{6}\) and \(\cot\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
solution: At \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\), cosine is \(\frac12\). Its reciprocal is \(\sec\frac{5\pi}{3}=2\).
At \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\), sine is \(-\frac12\). Its reciprocal is \(\cosec\frac{7\pi}{6}=-2\).
At \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\), cosine is zero and sine is \(-1\). Therefore \(\cot\frac{3\pi}{2}=0\).

examples.title: Read one branch of cotangent
examples.question: Describe \(y=\cot x\) on \(0\le x\le\pi\).
solution: Sine vanishes at both ends, so \(x=0\) and \(x=\pi\) are vertical asymptotes.
At \(x=\frac\pi2\), cosine is zero and sine is one. The branch crosses the axis here.
Between the asymptotes sine is positive. The ratio decreases from large positive values to large negative values through the crossing.

examples.title: Find tangent from a signed secant
examples.question: Angle \(x\) is in quadrant III and \(\sec x=-\frac53\). Find \(\tan x\) exactly.
solution: The identity gives \(\tan^2x=\frac{25}{9}-1=\frac{16}{9}\).
Sine and cosine are both negative in quadrant III, so tangent is positive.
Choose \(\tan x=\frac43\).

examples.title: Solve a secant equation in radians
examples.question: Solve \(\sec x=-\sqrt2\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
solution: The equation gives \(\cos x=-\frac1{\sqrt2}=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\).
The reference angle is \(\frac\pi4\). Negative cosine occurs in quadrants II and III.
The solutions are \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\). At both angles cosine is non-zero.

examples.title: Use the reciprocal of sin
examples.question: Find the exact value of \(\operatorname{cosec}240^\circ\).
solution: First find the signed value of \(\sin240^\circ\), which is \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
Take its reciprocal to obtain \(- \frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}\). The sign stays the same.

examples.title: Find both exclusions for a shifted reciprocal
examples.question: For \(0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\), find all inputs where \(\sec\left((x - 30)^\circ\right)\) is undefined. Enter angles in degrees.
solution: The denominator is \(\cos\left((x - 30)^\circ\right)\). List its zeros in the shifted interval.
Adding back the shift gives \(120^\circ\), \(300^\circ\).

examples.title: Find both exclusions for a shifted reciprocal
examples.question: For \(0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\), find all inputs where \(\operatorname{cosec}\left((x - 15)^\circ\right)\) is undefined. Enter angles in degrees.
solution: The denominator is \(\sin\left((x - 15)^\circ\right)\). List its zeros in the shifted interval.
Adding back the shift gives \(15^\circ\), \(195^\circ\).

revision.body:
Write the definitions

\(\sec x=\frac1{\cos x}\), \(\cosec x=\frac1{\sin x}\), \(\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\). Check the denominator first.

Read the graphs

Use integer \(k\) to locate each excluded input. Secant and cosecant have no zeros.

RatioAsymptotesPeriodRange
Secant\(x=\frac\pi2+k\pi\)\(2\pi\)\(|y|\ge1\)
Cosecant\(x=k\pi\)\(2\pi\)\(|y|\ge1\)
Cotangent\(x=k\pi\)\(\pi\)All real values

Cotangent crosses the axis at \(x=\frac\pi2+k\pi\).

Choose a squared identity

\(\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x\) and \(\cosec^2x=1+\cot^2x\). Use the quadrant to choose a sign.
revision.checks:
• Locate the forbidden inputs.
  • Choose the sign after finding a square.
  • List every solution in the interval.
revision.examTip: \(\cot x=0\) is solved using \(\cos x=0\) and \(\sin x\ne0\). Taking \(\frac1{\cot x}\) at a zero would be undefined.

orig_9709_p3_trig_compound_angles.description: Use the sine, cosine and tangent addition formulae for exact values and expressions.

sections.title: How do sine and cosine treat a sum or difference?
sections.label: Expand sine and cosine
sections.intro: First choose the function on the left. Sine combines the cross-products and uses the sign inside the argument. Cosine pairs the cosines and the sines. Its sign between those two terms is reversed.

blocks.html:
\(\sin(A\pm B)=\sin A\cos B\pm\cos A\sin B\)

\(\cos(A\pm B)=\cos A\cos B\mp\sin A\sin B\)
\(\sin(A+B)\) is a sum of products. Adding \(\sin A\) and \(\sin B\) can even give a value above one.

blocks.title: Build an exact value from known angles
blocks.prompt: Find \(\sin105^\circ\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use \(105^\circ=60^\circ+45^\circ\). Both products in the sine expansion are positive.
blocks.solution: \(\sin105^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\).

retry.feedback: The sine sum formula adds the cross-products.

sections.title: How do I expand a tangent sum or difference?
sections.label: Expand tangent
sections.intro: The numerator takes the sign of the original bracket. The denominator uses the opposite sign. This formula comes from the sine expansion divided by the cosine expansion, after dividing top and bottom by \(\cos A\cos B\).

blocks.html: \(\tan(A\pm B)=\frac{\tan A\pm\tan B}{1\mp\tan A\tan B}\) when the tangents and quotient are defined.
If the individual tangents are undefined, expand sine and cosine separately and use their quotient when the expanded cosine is non-zero.

blocks.title: Use the difference formula
blocks.prompt: Find \(\tan\frac\pi{12}\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use \(\frac\pi{12}=\frac\pi4-\frac\pi6\). The denominator has a plus sign.
blocks.solution: \(\tan\frac\pi{12}=\frac{1-\frac1{\sqrt3}}{1+\frac1{\sqrt3}}=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1}=2-\sqrt3\).

retry.feedback: That value belongs to the sum. The argument here is a difference.

sections.title: How do I fill in missing ratios before expanding?
sections.label: Recover the missing sides
sections.intro: Use \(\sin^2 A+\cos^2 A=1\) to find a missing ratio. Its sign comes from the quadrant. For an acute angle both ratios are positive.

blocks.html: Put the ratios in two columns, one per angle, before substituting. This helps keep each sine and cosine with its own angle.

blocks.title: Recover two missing ratios
blocks.prompt: Angles \(A\) and \(B\) are acute, with \(\sin A=\frac8{17}\) and \(\cos B=\frac35\). Find \(\sin(A-B)\).
blocks.hint: Find \(\cos A\) and \(\sin B\) first. The sine difference formula subtracts the second cross-product.
blocks.solution: \(\cos A=\frac{15}{17}\) and \(\sin B=\frac45\). The difference is \(\frac{24}{85}-\frac{60}{85}=-\frac{36}{85}\).

retry.feedback: Check the order of the two angles. The term with sine A comes first.

sections.title: How do I collect terms with the same angle?
sections.label: Expand and collect
sections.intro: Expand each function before collecting the \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) terms. Keep an outside multiplier attached to both products.

blocks.title: Find both coefficients
blocks.prompt: Write \(2\sin(x-30^\circ)+\cos(x+60^\circ)\) as \(a\sin x+b\cos x\). Find \(a\) and \(b\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Expand the sine difference and the cosine sum separately. Group sine terms and cosine terms.
blocks.solution: The sine coefficient is \(\sqrt3-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). The cosine coefficient is \(-1+\frac12=-\frac12\).

retry.feedback: The sine term in the expansion of the cosine sum carries a minus sign.

sections.title: How can a difference give a special angle?
sections.label: Choose a useful split
sections.intro: Write the requested angle as a sum or difference of familiar angles.

blocks.html: Pick a split that gives exact sine and cosine values. Check the signs in the formula before substituting.
Cosine of a difference has the plus sign in the middle, while cosine of a sum has minus.

blocks.title: Expand a sin difference
blocks.prompt: Find \(\sin(120^\circ-45^\circ)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Choose the identity for the named trigonometric function, and check whether the angles are added or subtracted.
blocks.solution:
For this identity substitute \(A=120^\circ,\ B=45^\circ\) into \(\sin A\cos B-\cos A\sin B\).

Substitute the exact special-angle values before simplifying. The result is \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\).

glossary.definition: An angle written as a sum or difference, such as \(A-B\).
A value kept in an exact form such as a fraction or surd.
The multiplier in front of a term.

examples.title: Find an exact sine in degrees
examples.question: Find \(\sin15^\circ\) exactly.
solution: Use \(15^\circ=45^\circ-30^\circ\) so that every ratio in the expansion is known.
\(\sin15^\circ=\sin45^\circ\cos30^\circ-\cos45^\circ\sin30^\circ\).
Substitute the exact values to obtain \(\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\).

examples.title: Use a tangent sum and simplify
examples.question: Find \(\tan75^\circ\) exactly.
solution: Write \(75^\circ=45^\circ+30^\circ\). The sum gives numerator \(1+\frac1{\sqrt3}\) and denominator \(1-\frac1{\sqrt3}\).
Multiply both by \(\sqrt3\) to obtain \(\frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3-1}\).
Multiply the top and bottom by \(\sqrt3+1\). The denominator becomes two and the value is \(2+\sqrt3\).

examples.title: Use known ratios for two acute angles
examples.question: Angles \(A\) and \(B\) are acute, with \(\sin A=\frac5{13}\) and \(\cos B=\frac45\). Find \(\cos(A+B)\).
solution: The unit identity gives \(\cos A=\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\sin B=\frac35\), using the positive roots.
Use \(\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B\). The two products are \(\frac{48}{65}\) and \(\frac{15}{65}\).
The difference is \(\frac{33}{65}\).

examples.title: Combine a cosine difference with a sine sum
examples.question: Write \(2\cos(x-60^\circ)-\sin(x+30^\circ)\) in terms of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\).
solution: Expand the first term to \(\cos x+\sqrt3\sin x\), using the plus in the cosine difference.
Expand the subtracted expression to \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin x+\frac12\cos x\).
Subtract each coefficient. The result is \(\frac12\cos x+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin x\).

examples.title: Expand a cos sum
examples.question: Find \(\cos(45^\circ+30^\circ)\) exactly.
solution: For this identity substitute \(A=45^\circ,\ B=30^\circ\) into \(\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B\).
Substitute the exact special-angle values before simplifying. The result is \(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\).

examples.title: Expand a tan difference
examples.question: Find \(\tan(45^\circ-60^\circ)\) exactly.
solution: For this identity substitute \(A=45^\circ,\ B=60^\circ\) into \(\frac{\tan A-\tan B}{1+\tan A\tan B}\).
Substitute the exact special-angle values before simplifying. The result is \(-2 + \sqrt{3}\).

examples.title: Expand a cos difference
examples.question: Find \(\cos(60^\circ-45^\circ)\) exactly.
solution: For this identity substitute \(A=60^\circ,\ B=45^\circ\) into \(\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B\).
Substitute the exact special-angle values before simplifying. The result is \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\).

revision.body:
Read the signs

\(\sin(A\pm B)=\sin A\cos B\pm\cos A\sin B\)

\(\cos(A\pm B)=\cos A\cos B\mp\sin A\sin B\)

\(\tan(A\pm B)=\frac{\tan A\pm\tan B}{1\mp\tan A\tan B}\) when both sides exist.

Build exact values

Choose familiar angles. For example \(15^\circ=45^\circ-30^\circ\), giving \(\sin15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\).

Convert and collect

Use the quadrant to recover a missing sine or cosine. Expand the brackets and collect the coefficients of the same trigonometric function.
revision.checks:
• Check the sign in the cosine formula.
  • Check the tangent denominator.
  • Multiply through every term in a bracket.
revision.examTip: If asked for an exact value, use exact ratios for the two angles and simplify before using a calculator to check.

Substitute the exact special-angle values before simplifying. The result is \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

orig_9709_p3_trig_double_angles.description: Choose a double-angle formula, reduce squared terms and solve equations across the full transformed interval.

sections.title: What changes when both angles are the same?
sections.label: Double the angle
sections.intro: Set \(A=B=x\) in the compound formulae. The two sine products are then identical, so they add to \(2\sin x\cos x\).

blocks.html: \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\). Squaring \(\sin x\) would give \(\sin^2x\), a different expression.

blocks.title: Keep the sign of both factors
blocks.prompt: Angle \(A\) is in quadrant IV and \(\cos A=\frac{15}{17}\). Find \(\sin2A\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use the negative square root for \(\sin A\), then multiply both ratios.

retry.feedback: Sine is negative in quadrant IV.
The two cross-products in the sine sum are identical. Include both.

sections.title: Which cosine formula removes the unwanted square?
sections.label: Choose a cosine form
sections.intro: The original cosine sum gives \(\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x\). Replace one squared term with the unit identity, depending on which ratio you already know.

blocks.html: \(\cos2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x\). These give \(\cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos2x}{2}\) and \(\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}\).
To collect terms, for instance \(4\sin^2x+3\cos2x=2(1-\cos2x)+3\cos2x=2+\cos2x\).

blocks.title: Select the formula using cosine only
blocks.prompt: Given \(\cos A=\frac27\), find \(\cos2A\).

retry.feedback: The cosine-only formula is twice the square minus one.

sections.title: When can I use the tangent formula?
sections.label: Use the double tangent
sections.intro: The tangent sum with equal angles gives \(\tan2x=\frac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2x}\). Check both that \(\tan x\) exists and that the denominator is non-zero.

blocks.html: If \(\tan x\) is undefined, this form is unavailable. At \(x=\frac\pi2\), \(\tan2x=\tan\pi=0\) can still be evaluated directly.

blocks.title: A negative denominator changes the sign
blocks.prompt: Given \(\tan A=2\), find \(\tan2A\).
blocks.hint: The denominator is \(1-4\).

retry.feedback: Keep the sign of the denominator.
The double-angle tangent denominator is one minus the square.

sections.title: Why do I double the interval before solving?
sections.label: Solve in the new interval
sections.intro: Let \(u=2x\) and transform both bounds. Find every allowed \(u\) before dividing by two. Keep the original inclusion at each endpoint.

blocks.html: An interval of length \(2\pi\) in \(x\) has length \(4\pi\) in \(2x\). That covers two full sine and cosine cycles.

blocks.title: Solve for the angle inside sine first
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin2x=-\frac12\) for \(0\le x<\pi\). Give all answers exactly.
blocks.hint: In \(0\le u<2\pi\), sine is negative in quadrants III and IV.
blocks.solution: The solutions for \(u=2x\) are \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\). Dividing by two gives \(x=\frac{7\pi}{12}\) or \(x=\frac{11\pi}{12}\).

retry.feedback: These are values of the doubled angle. Divide both by two.
Find the second negative sine angle in the transformed interval.

sections.title: How many cycles does the doubled interval include?
sections.label: Check both families
sections.intro: Doubling the angle doubles the size of its interval.

blocks.html: Find both sine patterns in the expanded interval, then divide each solution by the matching scale.
One full cycle in the original variable can contain two or more cycles of the transformed angle.

blocks.title: Find every root after stretching the interval
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin(2x^\circ)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter all angles in degrees.
blocks.hint: Convert the interval as well as the equation, and keep both sine families.
blocks.solution:
Let \(u=2x\), giving \(0\le u<720\). The reference angle is \(45^\circ\).

The sine equation gives the angle families \(u=45+360k,\quad u=135+360k\).

Retain all values in the expanded interval. Divide each by \(2\) to obtain \(\frac{45}{2}^\circ\), \(\frac{135}{2}^\circ\), \(\frac{405}{2}^\circ\), \(\frac{495}{2}^\circ\).

glossary.definition: An argument twice the original one, such as \(2x\).
The square of a value, such as \(\sin^2x=(\sin x)^2\).
The allowed interval for the whole angle after substitution.

examples.title: Double a sine with a negative cosine
examples.question: Angle \(A\) is in quadrant II and \(\sin A=\frac7{25}\). Find \(\sin2A\).
solution: The squared cosine is \(1-\frac{49}{625}=\frac{576}{625}\). Cosine is negative in quadrant II.
\(\cos A=-\frac{24}{25}\). Apply the double-angle formula.

examples.title: Calculate a cosine using only sine
examples.question: Given \(\sin A=\frac35\), find \(\cos2A\).
solution: With sine already known, choose \(\cos2A=1-2\sin^2A\). No quadrant is needed for the squared term.

examples.title: Double an angle when the tangent is negative
examples.question: Given \(\tan A=-\frac13\), find \(\tan2A\).
solution: The denominator is \(1-\frac19=\frac89\), so the formula applies.
\(\tan2A=\frac{-\frac23}{\frac89}=-\frac34\).

examples.title: Find the roots over two cycles
examples.question: Solve \(\cos2x=\frac12\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: Let \(u=2x\). The new interval is \(0\le u\le4\pi\).
One cycle gives \(u=\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}{3}\). Adding \(2\pi\) to each gives \(\frac{7\pi}{3},\frac{11\pi}{3}\).
Halve each angle to obtain \(x=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}{6},\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{11\pi}{6}\). Neither endpoint solves the equation.

examples.title: Use both exact double-angle values
examples.question: Given \(\sin\theta=\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta<0\), find \(\sin(2\theta)\) and \(\cos(2\theta)\) exactly.
solution: Use \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) and the sign condition. This gives \(\sin\theta=\frac{4}{5},\quad\cos\theta=- \frac{3}{5}\).
Use \(\sin(2\theta)=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) and \(\cos(2\theta)=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta\) to get \(- \frac{24}{25}\) and \(- \frac{7}{25}\).

examples.title: Retain the sign of the double-angle denominator
examples.question: Given \(\tan\theta=\frac{7}{3}\), find \(\tan(2\theta)\) exactly.
solution: The numerator \(2\tan\theta\) is \(\frac{14}{3}\) and the denominator \(1-\tan^2\theta\) is \(- \frac{40}{9}\).
Divide to get \(- \frac{21}{20}\). The denominator is non-zero, so the double-angle tangent exists.

examples.title: Find every root after stretching the interval
examples.question: Solve \(\sin(2x^\circ)=- \frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter all angles in degrees.
solution: Let \(u=2x\), giving \(0\le u<720\). The reference angle is \(30^\circ\).
The sine equation gives the angle families \(u=-30+360k,\quad u=210+360k\).
Retain all values in the expanded interval. Divide each by \(2\) to obtain \(105^\circ\), \(165^\circ\), \(285^\circ\), \(345^\circ\).

revision.body:
Double the argument

\(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\), \(\tan2x=\frac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2x}\) where the right-hand side is defined.

Choose a cosine identity

\(\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x\). Choose the form containing the ratio already given.

Reduce squared terms

\(\cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos2x}{2}\), \(\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}\).

Solve over the right interval

With \(u=2x\), double both endpoints, find every \(u\) in the new interval, then halve the solutions.
revision.checks:
• Keep the sign of both factors in double sine.
  • Check the double tangent denominator.
  • Count the cycles after transforming the bounds.
revision.examTip: \(\sin^2x\) squares the output. \(\sin2x\) doubles the input. Decide which one appears before choosing a formula.

orig_9709_p3_trig_r_form.description: Combine sine and cosine into one wave, check the phase and use the result for bounds and equations.

sections.title: How can I combine two ratios into one sine?
sections.label: Match a sine wave
sections.intro: Expand the requested bracket first. For \(R\sin(x+\alpha)\), the sine coefficient is \(R\cos\alpha\) and the cosine coefficient is \(R\sin\alpha\). Match the two coefficients and square and add to find \(R\).

blocks.html: \(R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) when combining \(a\sin x+b\cos x\) with at least one non-zero coefficient. The signs of \(\sin\alpha\) and \(\cos\alpha\) must fit the requested form.

blocks.title: Match a negative cosine coefficient
blocks.prompt: Write \(5\sin x-12\cos x\) as \(R\sin(x-\alpha)\), with \(R>0\) and \(0<\alpha<\frac\pi2\). Give \(R\) and \(\alpha\) exactly.
blocks.hint: The minus in the bracket accounts for the negative cosine coefficient. Find \(R\cos\alpha\) and \(R\sin\alpha\).
blocks.solution: \(R\cos\alpha=5\), \(R\sin\alpha=12\). Thus \(R=13\) and \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)\).

retry.feedback: Square and add the coefficients instead of adding their magnitudes.

sections.title: Why does the phase sign change in the cosine form?
sections.label: Match a cosine wave
sections.intro: Expand \(R\cos(x-\alpha)\) to get \(R\cos\alpha\cos x+R\sin\alpha\sin x\). A plus sign in the cosine bracket instead gives a negative sine term for acute \(\alpha\).

blocks.html: For \(3\cos x+4\sin x\), \(R=5\) and \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac43\right)\) in \(R\cos(x-\alpha)\). At \(x=\alpha\), the shifted argument is zero.

figure.alt: Two cosine waves of amplitude five. The dashed reference curve peaks at zero. The solid wave peaks later, at alpha, and reaches its trough at alpha plus pi.
figure.caption: Both curves have amplitude \(5\). The peak of \(5\cos(x-\alpha)\) is shifted right by \(\alpha\).

blocks.html: A tangent ratio alone can leave a quadrant ambiguous. Check both coefficient equations after choosing a phase. If one coefficient is zero, use the coefficient equations directly.

blocks.title: Read both coefficients in the cosine form
blocks.prompt: Write \(20\cos x+21\sin x\) as \(R\cos(x-\alpha)\), with \(R>0\) and \(0<\alpha<\frac\pi2\). Give \(R\) and \(\alpha\) exactly.
blocks.hint: For the difference form, the sine coefficient is \(R\sin\alpha\).
blocks.solution: \(R=\sqrt{20^2+21^2}=29\). The phase is \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{21}{20}\right)\).

sections.title: What can the amplitude tell me about maxima and minima?
sections.label: Read the range
sections.intro: With \(R>0\), \(R\sin(x+\alpha)\) and \(R\cos(x-\alpha)\) take values from \(-R\) to \(R\) over a full cycle. A vertical shift \(c\) moves both endpoints by \(c\).

blocks.html: On a restricted interval, check which peaks and troughs occur there and compare the endpoint values. The full-cycle range may be too wide.

blocks.title: Find both bounds of a shifted wave
blocks.prompt: Find the range of \(g(x)=5+8\cos x+15\sin x\) for all real \(x\).
blocks.hint: Find the amplitude from the two coefficients, then apply the vertical shift.
blocks.solution: \(R=17\), so the range is \(-12\le g(x)\le22\).

retry.feedback: The amplitude is correct. Apply the vertical shift to both endpoints.

sections.title: How do I solve an equation after finding the R form?
sections.label: Solve the shifted equation
sections.intro: Divide by \(R\) and check that the target lies between \(-1\) and \(1\). Then use the interval for the whole shifted angle. Undo the shift on every solution and check the original endpoints.

blocks.html: With \(u=x-\alpha\), subtract \(\alpha\) from both bounds. Convert a candidate back with \(x=u+\alpha\).

blocks.title: Include the correct endpoint only
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sqrt3\sin x+\cos x=1\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\). Give all answers exactly.
blocks.hint: Use \(2\sin(x+\frac\pi6)\) and move both bounds by \(\frac\pi6\).
blocks.solution: Put \(u=x+\frac\pi6\). Within \(\frac\pi6\le u<\frac{13\pi}{6}\), \(\sin u=\frac12\) at \(u=\frac\pi6\) and \(u=\frac{5\pi}{6}\). Hence \(x=0\) or \(x=\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

retry.feedback: The upper endpoint is excluded. Check the strict inequality.
These values are for the shifted angle. Subtract pi over six.

sections.title: How do the original signs locate the phase?
sections.label: Read both phase ratios
sections.intro: A tangent alone can correspond to angles separated by a half-turn.

blocks.html: Match both the sine and cosine ratios of the phase with their signs. An amplitude is positive.
Taking an acute angle automatically can give coefficients of the wrong sign.

blocks.title: Read the phase and amplitude from two coefficients
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(\theta)=- 21 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} - 20 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\). Write the variable part as \(R\cos(\theta-\alpha)\) with \(0\le\alpha<2\pi\). Give \(R,\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Square and add the two coefficients. Use their original signs when reading phase ratios.
blocks.solution:
Expanding \(R\cos(\theta-\alpha)\) against cosine and sine gives \(R\cos\alpha=-20,\quad R\sin\alpha=-21\).

Squaring and adding gives \(R=29\). The phase ratios are \(\cos\alpha=- \frac{20}{29},\quad\sin\alpha=- \frac{21}{29}\).

With the vertical shift included, the full range is \([-29,29]\).

glossary.definition: The distance from the middle line to a peak, equal to \(R\).
The angle in the bracket that sets the horizontal shift.
An expression written as a single shifted sine or cosine.

examples.title: Match and check a sine sum
examples.question: Write \(8\sin x+15\cos x\) as \(R\sin(x+\alpha)\), where \(R>0\) and \(\alpha\) is acute.
solution: Comparing coefficients gives \(R\cos\alpha=8\) and \(R\sin\alpha=15\).
Square and add to get \(R^2=8^2+15^2=289\), so \(R=17\).
Divide the equations to get \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{15}{8}\right)\). Both ratios are positive, as needed for the acute phase.

examples.title: Choose a cosine sum with a negative sine coefficient
examples.question: Write \(12\cos x-5\sin x\) as \(R\cos(x+\alpha)\), where \(R>0\) and \(\alpha\) is acute.
solution: The cosine sum expands to \(R\cos\alpha\cos x-R\sin\alpha\sin x\). Compare it with the given coefficients.
\(R\cos\alpha=12\), \(R\sin\alpha=5\). Hence \(R=13\) and \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac5{12}\right)\).
The plus inside the bracket produces the required minus in front of \(\sin x\).

examples.title: Find both extrema without differentiation
examples.question: Give the minimum and maximum of \(4+6\sin x-8\cos x\) over all real \(x\).
solution: The sine and cosine terms combine into a wave of amplitude \(\sqrt{6^2+(-8)^2}=10\).
The range of that wave is \([-10,10]\). Add four to both endpoints.
The minimum is \(-6\) and the maximum is \(14\).

examples.title: Solve using the shifted cosine interval
examples.question: Solve \(3\cos x+3\sqrt3\sin x=-3\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
solution: The left side is \(6\cos(x-\frac\pi3)\). Put \(u=x-\frac\pi3\) so \(-\frac\pi3\le u<\frac{5\pi}{3}\).
\(\cos u=-\frac12\) gives \(u=\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3}\) in this interval.
Add \(\frac\pi3\) to get \(x=\pi\) or \(x=\frac{5\pi}{3}\).

examples.title: Read the phase and amplitude from two coefficients
examples.question: Let \(f(\theta)=15 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 8 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\). Write the variable part as \(R\cos(\theta-\alpha)\) with \(0\le\alpha<2\pi\). Give \(R,\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha\) exactly.
solution: Expanding \(R\cos(\theta-\alpha)\) against cosine and sine gives \(R\cos\alpha=8,\quad R\sin\alpha=15\).
Squaring and adding gives \(R=17\). The phase ratios are \(\cos\alpha=\frac{8}{17},\quad\sin\alpha=\frac{15}{17}\).
With the vertical shift included, the full range is \([-17,17]\).

examples.title: Read the phase and amplitude from two coefficients
examples.question: Let \(f(\theta)=- 5 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 12 \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4\). Find the minimum and maximum value.
solution: Expanding \(R\cos(\theta-\alpha)\) against cosine and sine gives \(R\cos\alpha=12,\quad R\sin\alpha=-5\).
Squaring and adding gives \(R=13\). The phase ratios are \(\cos\alpha=\frac{12}{13},\quad\sin\alpha=- \frac{5}{13}\).
With the vertical shift included, the full range is \([-9,17]\).

examples.title: Read the phase and amplitude from two coefficients
examples.question: Let \(f(\theta)=24 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} - 7 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\). Write the variable part as \(R\cos(\theta-\alpha)\) with \(0\le\alpha<2\pi\). Give \(R,\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha\) exactly.
solution: Expanding \(R\cos(\theta-\alpha)\) against cosine and sine gives \(R\cos\alpha=-7,\quad R\sin\alpha=24\).
Squaring and adding gives \(R=25\). The phase ratios are \(\cos\alpha=- \frac{7}{25},\quad\sin\alpha=\frac{24}{25}\).
With the vertical shift included, the full range is \([-25,25]\).

revision.body:
Find the amplitude

\(R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) for a non-zero combination of \(a\sin x+b\cos x\).

Expand and match

\(R\sin(x\pm\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\sin x\pm R\sin\alpha\cos x\).

\(R\cos(x\pm\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\cos x\mp R\sin\alpha\sin x\).

Read the bounds and solve

Over a complete cycle a vertical shift \(c\) gives range \([c-R,c+R]\). To solve an equation, transfer both interval bounds to the shifted angle and convert each solution back.
revision.checks:
• Find the positive amplitude.
  • Expand the chosen form to check both coefficient signs.
  • Keep the same endpoint inclusion.
revision.examTip: Use an exact phase where possible. If a decimal angle is needed, keep the unrounded phase until after solving.

orig_9709_p3_trig_equations.description: Select an identity, preserve the original restrictions and find every solution in the specified interval.

sections.title: How do I decide which side to rewrite?
sections.label: Prove an identity
sections.intro: Start with the side that offers a clear simplification. Look for a double angle, a square or a reciprocal. Aim to produce the other side through reversible steps on the common domain.

blocks.html: An identity must hold for every input where the expressions are defined. A test at a single angle can catch an error but cannot establish the identity.

blocks.title: Recognise a cosine double-angle form
blocks.prompt: For inputs where \(\sin 2x\ne0\), which ratio equals \(\frac{1+\cos2x}{\sin2x}\)?
blocks.hint: Use the form of \(\cos2x\) containing \(\cos^2x\), then cancel.
blocks.solution: The fraction becomes \(\frac{2\cos^2x}{2\sin x\cos x}=\cot x\) on the stated domain.

retry.feedback: Tangent is sine divided by cosine. Here cosine remains in the numerator.

sections.title: How do I keep a branch that division would lose?
sections.label: Factor and keep both branches
sections.intro: When an equation contains a repeated trigonometric factor, bring all terms to one side. Set each factor equal to zero, solve each equation, then combine the solutions.

blocks.html: Dividing by \(\sin x\) would require \(\sin x\ne0\). Factorising keeps its zero branch visible.

blocks.title: Retain the solutions where sine is zero
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin2x=\sqrt2\sin x\) for \(-\pi\le x<\pi\). Give all solutions exactly.
blocks.hint: With \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\), take \(\sin x\) out as a factor.
blocks.solution: \(\sin x(2\cos x-\sqrt2)=0\). The first factor gives \(x=-\pi,0\). The second gives \(x=-\frac\pi4,\frac\pi4\).

retry.feedback: Also solve the first factor. Dividing by sine would have discarded its zeros.
The positive endpoint is excluded.

sections.title: Which candidates survive the original restrictions?
sections.label: Check the original domain
sections.intro: Write down where each original denominator vanishes. Keep these exclusions if you cancel a factor. If you square an equation, check the candidates in the unsquared equation as well.

blocks.html: If all candidates are excluded, say that there are no solutions and give the reason.

blocks.title: Cancel only on the allowed inputs
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\frac{\cos 2x-1}{\sin x}=-\sqrt2\) for \(0\le x\le 2\pi\). Give all solutions exactly.
blocks.hint: Write the numerator as \(-2\sin^2x\) and use the original requirement \(\sin x\ne0\).
blocks.solution: On its original domain the equation becomes \(\sin x=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), so \(x=\frac\pi4\) or \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\). Neither value makes the denominator zero.

retry.feedback: Positive sine also occurs in quadrant II.

sections.title: How do I solve a quadratic in one ratio?
sections.label: Solve the quadratic first
sections.intro: If an equation includes \(\cos2x\) and \(\sin x\), use \(\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x\). Let \(s=\sin x\) and solve the quadratic. Retain only values in \(-1\le s\le1\) before finding angles.

blocks.html: Solve an equation for each retained ratio. Repeated angle values go in the final list only once.

blocks.title: Discard an impossible sine value
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cos2x+5\sin x=3\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\). Give all solutions exactly.
blocks.hint: Write \(2s^2-5s+2=0\) for \(s=\sin x\). Only one root is in the range of sine.
blocks.solution: \((2s-1)(s-2)=0\). Reject \(s=2\) and solve \(\sin x=\frac12\), giving \(x=\frac\pi6\) or \(x=\frac{5\pi}{6}\).

retry.feedback: Find the second angle with the same sine in the interval.

sections.title: How can I track a shifted interval across more than one cycle?
sections.label: Shift and scale the bounds
sections.intro: Name the entire argument \(u=ax+b\). Map both bounds before finding roots. If \(a\) is negative, the smaller and larger endpoints swap and inequality signs reverse. Use a periodic sketch or a reference angle and repeat by the correct period.

blocks.html: Work with every complete or partial cycle covered by the transformed interval.

figure.alt: Sine from minus 90 degrees to 390 degrees. It meets the horizontal line of height one half at 30, 150 and the included right endpoint 390 degrees.
figure.caption: For \(u=2x+30^\circ\) and \(-60^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\), the horizontal line \(y=\frac12\) meets the plotted curve at all three allowed angles.

blocks.title: Check both shifted endpoints
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cos(2x-60^\circ)=\frac12\) for \(-120^\circ\le x<180^\circ\). Give all solutions in degrees.
blocks.hint: For \(u=2x-60^\circ\) the allowed interval is \(-300^\circ\le u<300^\circ\).
blocks.solution: Use \(u=\pm60^\circ+360^\circ k\), for integer \(k\). This gives \(u=-300^\circ,-60^\circ,60^\circ\). Convert back to get \(x=-120^\circ,0^\circ,60^\circ\).

sections.title: How do I reject impossible values of a trigonometric ratio?
sections.label: Use the range
sections.intro: An algebraic equation can have values outside the range of a sine or cosine.

blocks.html: Filter candidate ratios, then solve for every valid angle in the original interval.
Do not ask the calculator for an inverse sine of a value whose magnitude is greater than one.

blocks.title: Discard an algebraic root outside the sine range
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin^2(x^\circ) - \frac{3 \sin(x^\circ)}{2} - 1=0\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter angles in degrees.
blocks.hint: Filter the algebraic roots through the range of sine before solving for the angle.
blocks.solution:
Let \(u=\sin(x^\circ)\). The quadratic gives \(u=- \frac{1}{2}\text{ or }u=2\).

As \(-1\le u\le1\), keep \(- \frac{1}{2}\). The complete answer is \(210^\circ\), \(330^\circ\).

examples.title: Choose the form of cosine that exposes a factor
examples.question: Show that \(\frac{1-\cos2x}{\sin2x}=\tan x\) wherever the left side is defined.
solution: Use \(\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x\), which makes the numerator \(2\sin^2x\).
The denominator is \(2\sin x\cos x\), so both sine and cosine are non-zero on the original domain.
Cancel the common factor to give \(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\tan x\), with the original restrictions still in force.

examples.title: Keep the zeros of cosine
examples.question: Solve \(\sin2x=\cos x\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
solution: Use \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\) and bring the right side across.
\(\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0\). The first factor gives \(x=\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
The second factor gives \(\sin x=\frac12\), hence \(x=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}{6}\). Include all four.

examples.title: Reject an input excluded by a cancelled expression
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{2\sin^2x}{1-\cos x}=4\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: Require \(\cos x\ne1\). Factor \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x=(1-\cos x)(1+\cos x)\).
On the allowed domain the equation becomes \(2(1+\cos x)=4\), giving \(\cos x=1\).
The only candidates are \(0\) and \(2\pi\), both excluded by the original denominator. There are no solutions.

examples.title: Use one ratio before factorising
examples.question: Solve \(\cos2x+3\sin x=2\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
solution: Set \(s=\sin x\). Since \(\cos2x=1-2s^2\), rearrange to \(2s^2-3s+1=0\).
Factorise to \((2s-1)(s-1)=0\), so \(s=\frac12\) or \(s=1\). Both lie in the range of sine.
\(s=\frac12\) gives \(x=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}{6}\). The maximum value \(s=1\) occurs once, at \(x=\frac\pi2\).

examples.title: Use both interval endpoints before converting back
examples.question: Solve \(\sin(2x+30^\circ)=\frac12\) for \(-60^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\).
solution: Let \(u=2x+30^\circ\). The new interval is \(-90^\circ\le u\le390^\circ\).
Use \(u=30^\circ+360^\circ k\) or \(u=150^\circ+360^\circ k\) for integer \(k\). The values in range are \(30^\circ,150^\circ,390^\circ\).
Use \(x=\frac{u-30^\circ}{2}\) to obtain \(0^\circ,60^\circ,180^\circ\), including the right endpoint.

examples.title: Separate and solve both trigonometric factors
examples.question: Solve \(\sin(2(x-20)^\circ)=-\sin((x-20)^\circ)\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter your solutions in degrees.
solution: Use \(\sin(2u)=2\sin u\cos u\) with \(u=(x-20)\). Bring all terms to one side.
The factors are \(\sin(u^\circ)\) and \(2\cos(u^\circ)-(-1)\). Solve both equations in the proper intervals.
Return to the original input. The solutions are \(20^\circ\), \(140^\circ\), \(200^\circ\), \(260^\circ\).

examples.title: Discard an algebraic root outside the sine range
examples.question: Solve \(\sin^2(x^\circ) - 4 \sin(x^\circ) + 3=0\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter angles in degrees.
solution: Let \(u=\sin(x^\circ)\). The quadratic gives \(u=1\text{ or }u=3\).
As \(-1\le u\le1\), keep \(1\). The complete answer is \(90^\circ\).

revision.body:
Choose an identity that connects the ratios

Change reciprocals to sine and cosine. Expand \(\sin2x\) to expose a product, and choose the \(\cos2x\) form that leaves one squared ratio.

Keep every factor and its domain

For \(\sin2x=\cos x\), use \(\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0\). Solve both factors. A denominator restriction remains in force after cancellation.

Solve for one ratio

Express every term using one function and solve the resulting quadratic. Discard a sine or cosine value outside \([-1,1]\) before finding angles.

Check a shifted interval

For \(u=2x+30^\circ\), transform both bounds. Use the original inclusion at each endpoint and convert every solution back to \(x\).
revision.checks:
• Identify which angles make the original expression undefined.
  • Solve each factor or branch and count the cycles.
  • Check the endpoints after undoing the substitution.
revision.examTip: In a proof, show how one side becomes the other throughout their common domain. In an equation, check whether each candidate satisfies the original statement.

extraPractice.title: Separate and solve both trigonometric factors
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin(2(x-15)^\circ)=\sin((x-15)^\circ)\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter your solutions in degrees.
extraPractice.hint: Factoring preserves the cases where the sine alone is zero.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(\sin(2u)=2\sin u\cos u\) with \(u=(x-15)\). Bring all terms to one side.

The factors are \(\sin(u^\circ)\) and \(2\cos(u^\circ)-(1)\). Solve both equations in the proper intervals.

Return to the original input. The solutions are \(15^\circ\), \(75^\circ\), \(195^\circ\), \(315^\circ\).

extraPractice.title: Discard an algebraic root outside the sine range
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin^2(x^\circ) + \frac{5 \sin(x^\circ)}{2} - \frac{3}{2}=0\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter angles in degrees.
extraPractice.hint: Filter the algebraic roots through the range of sine before solving for the angle.
extraPractice.solution:
Let \(u=\sin(x^\circ)\). The quadratic gives \(u=\frac{1}{2}\text{ or }u=-3\).

As \(-1\le u\le1\), keep \(\frac{1}{2}\). The complete answer is \(30^\circ\), \(150^\circ\).

extraPractice.title: Find every root after stretching the interval
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin(3x^\circ)=- \frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x<120\). Enter all angles in degrees.
extraPractice.hint: Convert the interval as well as the equation, and keep both sine families.
extraPractice.solution:
Let \(u=3x\), giving \(0\le u<360\). The reference angle is \(30^\circ\).

The sine equation gives the angle families \(u=-30+360k,\quad u=210+360k\).

Retain all values in the expanded interval. Divide each by \(3\) to obtain \(70^\circ\), \(110^\circ\).

extraPractice.title: Separate and solve both trigonometric factors
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin(2(x-35)^\circ)=-\sin((x-35)^\circ)\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter your solutions in degrees.
extraPractice.hint: Factoring preserves the cases where the sine alone is zero.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(\sin(2u)=2\sin u\cos u\) with \(u=(x-35)\). Bring all terms to one side.

The factors are \(\sin(u^\circ)\) and \(2\cos(u^\circ)-(-1)\). Solve both equations in the proper intervals.

Return to the original input. The solutions are \(35^\circ\), \(155^\circ\), \(215^\circ\), \(275^\circ\).

extraPractice.title: Discard an algebraic root outside the sine range
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin^2(x^\circ) + 3 \sin(x^\circ) + 2=0\) for \(0\le x<360\). Enter angles in degrees.
extraPractice.hint: Filter the algebraic roots through the range of sine before solving for the angle.
extraPractice.solution:
Let \(u=\sin(x^\circ)\). The quadratic gives \(u=-1\text{ or }u=-2\).

As \(-1\le u\le1\), keep \(-1\). The complete answer is \(270^\circ\).

extraPractice.title: Find every root after stretching the interval
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin(3x^\circ)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) for \(0\le x<240\). Enter all angles in degrees.
extraPractice.hint: Convert the interval as well as the equation, and keep both sine families.
extraPractice.solution:
Let \(u=3x\), giving \(0\le u<720\). The reference angle is \(45^\circ\).

The sine equation gives the angle families \(u=45+360k,\quad u=135+360k\).

Retain all values in the expanded interval. Divide each by \(3\) to obtain \(15^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(135^\circ\), \(165^\circ\).
